text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 448:
Common lift pump. In the up-stroke of piston or bucket the lower valve opens and the valve in piston shuts; air is exhausted out of suction-pipe, and water rushes up to fill the vacuum. In down-stroke, lower valve is shut and valve in piston opens, and the water simply passes through the piston. The water above piston is lifted up, and runs over out of spout at each up-stroke. This pump cannot raise water over thirty feet high.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 448; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_448.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 450:
Ordinary force pump, with two valves. The cylinder is above water, and is fitted with solid piston; one valve closes outlet-pipe, and other closes suction-pipe. When piston is rising suction-valve is open, and water rushes into cylinder, outlet-valve being closed. On descent of piston suction-valve closes, and water is forced up through outlet-valve to any distance or elevation.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 450; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_450.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 451:
Force pump, same as above, with addition of air-chamber to the outlet, to produce a constant flow. The outlet from air-chamber is shown at two places, from either of which water may be taken. The air is compressed by the water during the downward stroke of the piston, and expands and presses out the water from the chamber during the up-stroke.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 451; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_451.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 452:
Double-acting pump. Cylinder closed at each end, and piston-rod passes through stuffing-box on one end, and the cylinder has four openings covered by valves, two for admitting water and like number for discharge. A is suction-pipe, and B discharge-pipe. When piston moves down, water rushes in at suction-valve, 1, on upper end of cylinder, and that below piston is forced through valve, 3, and discharge-pipe, B; on the piston ascending again, water is forced through discharge-valve, 4, on upper end of cylinder, and water enters lower suction-valve, 2.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 452; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_452.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 453:
Double lantern-bellows pump. As one bellows is distended by lever, air is rarefied within it, and water passes up suction-pipe to fill space; at same time other bellows is compressed, and expels its contents through discharge-pipe; valves working the same as in the ordinary force pump.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 453; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_453.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 454:
Diaphragm forcing pump. A flexible diaphragm is employed instead of bellows, and valves are arranged same as in preceding.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 454; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_454.html.

text:
Henry T. Brown (1908), movement 465:
Balance pumps. Pair worked reciprocally by a person pressing alternately on opposite ends of lever or beam.
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 465; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_465.html.
